Now the snare sounds like a cardboard box, three songs of drums go down today, and the drummer, the assistant and the owner each have a different culprit.  ⚑ RV-176: the kit is Dez’s. RV-177: figures illustrative. Some choices run on a clock — and some depend on your loadout.

items.title: Phase at the Drum Kit
items.stakes: Dez's snare sounds like a cardboard box, and three songs of drums go down today.
items.reward: A snare with its body back — in stereo, in mono and in Dez's ears.

objectives.text: Decide how to fix the distance
Decide who checks it next time

items.rumor: Four good mics can add up to a worse drum.

items.alt: The live room: the drum kit in the middle under two overhead microphones; Dez points at the snare; Maya listens.

bubbles.text: Forty bucks on that head. Sounds like I'm hitting a parcel.
Hit it again. Just the top mic up, this time.

items.caption: Three songs of drums today.

lines.text: Forty bucks on that head. Sounds like I'm hitting a parcel.
Hit it for me. Then again, with just the top mic up.

items.prompt: 10:15. Dez blames the new head, Pim the preamp. Drums at one. What first?
unknown: Which mic takes the body away
items.risk: Three songs of drums with no snare.
timeout: Drums go down at one with the snare as it is.

hints.text: If the fault were the drum, would the close mic alone sound thin?

options.label: Swap the snare head back
options.result: Forty minutes, and it still sounds like cardboard.
options.consequence: Changes the instrument before listening to the microphones.

options.label: Listen to each snare mic alone, then add the others one at a time and hear where the body goes
options.result: Close mic alone: full. Add the bottom — thinner. Add the overheads — thinner again.
options.consequence: Find where the fault appears before you change anything.

options.label: Boost 200 Hz on the snare by 8 dB
options.consequence: EQ on top of a cancellation.

options.label: Swap the preamp, as Pim suggests

items.title: Top and bottom.
items.body: The body drops out the moment the bottom mic comes up. The bottom mic faces up at the same skin the top mic faces down at: as the head moves toward one it moves away from the other. The template used to flip it. Two years ago the template was rebuilt for the new desk — routing checked, polarity not. Maya flips it, and most of the body comes back.
items.label: Test: why do the top and bottom mics start out opposed?

items.label: **Order it:** line up a drum kit.

items.alt: A sheet with two parts. Left: a schematic of the snare with its close mic 5 cm above it, the bottom mic below it marked polarity not flipped, and two overheads — left at 1.20 m, right at 0.95 m. Right: the close mic plus the left overhead, compared with the close mic alone, from 50 Hz to 1 kHz — a comb with notches at 149, 447 and 746 Hz.
items.caption: Most of the body back — and a comb where the rest should be.

items.title: 2022 · ‘rebuilt for new desk’
items.body: The session template's notes: ‘2022 — rebuilt for new desk. Routing checked.’ Routing, yes. Polarity isn't routing. Nobody checked it.

items.title: Two microphones in one place
items.body: In 1931 Alan Blumlein, an engineer at a London record company, filed a patent for what he called binaural sound — stereo. One of his ideas was to put two figure-of-eight microphones at the same point, angled apart, so that every sound reaches both at the same instant. No time difference, no comb filter when the two are added. Engineers still set up a ‘Blumlein pair’ for the same reason.

items.text: Act II — “One point one five metres”

items.title: One point one five metres.
items.body: With the bottom flipped, the snare is fuller — until the overheads come up. Maya runs a tape from each overhead to the snare: 1.20 m on the left, 0.95 m on the right, 5 cm for the close mic. The same hit reaches the left overhead 3.35 ms after the close mic, and added together they cancel at 149 Hz, 447 Hz and 746 Hz — right where a snare's body lives. The overheads don't even agree with each other.
items.label: Test: how late is the overhead — and where is the first notch?

items.alt: The live room; Pim holds a tape measure stretched toward the kit; Dez watches from behind the snare.

bubbles.text: One-twenty on the left. Ninety-five on the right.
So my snare's in two places at once?

items.prompt: So you're telling me my drum was fine the whole time?

options.label: “Your drum was fine. We were listening to it through four mics that disagreed about when it happened.”
options.reply: Four mics arguing. That's every band I've been in.

options.label: “Mostly. The head's a bit bright.”
options.reply: …You're going to be one of those, aren't you.

items.prompt: Bottom mic flipped. The overheads still take the body. What now?
items.risk: Three songs of drums with a hollow snare.
timeout: Drums go down with the comb in them.

hints.text: Which part of this is a flip, and which part is a delay?

options.label: Mute the overheads and use close mics only
options.result: A snare with no room around it — and no cymbals.
options.consequence: Removes the problem and half the kit's sound.

options.label: With Dez's OK: set both overheads to 1.05 m from the snare, delay the close mics about 2.9 ms to line up with them, check in mono and ask Dez to listen
options.result: The snare sits in the middle and keeps its body with everything up. Mono holds.
options.consequence: Geometry first, then time, then the player's ears.

options.label: Move the close mic further from the snare to ‘blend’
options.result: More spill from the hi-hat and a new comb.

options.label: Flip the overheads' polarity as well
options.result: The notches move; the body doesn't come back.
options.consequence: A flip can't fix a delay.

items.text: ✦ UX RULE #94 · AVERY'S LENS  Every mic on one source hears it at a different time  When two microphones hear the same drum, their sum depends on polarity and on distance. Check polarity first, then distance — then let the player judge the sound.  A snare lost its body because its bottom mic was in opposite polarity and its overhead was a metre and fifteen further away.

items.alt: The same sheet after the fix: both overheads at 1.05 m, the bottom mic's polarity flipped, and on the right a flat green line — close mic and overhead aligned in time add evenly, 4.6 dB up at every frequency — over the old red comb.
items.caption: One drum, arriving once.

items.title: ‘OH to snare: equal. MEASURE.’
items.body: A laminated sheet from the nineties in Hollis's drawer: ‘Overheads to snare: EQUAL. MEASURE, don't guess. Flip the bottom.’ It had been in the drawer for twenty years.

items.prompt: Tomorrow a session drummer comes in for two songs. Who makes sure this doesn't happen again?
items.risk: The same comb, the next drummer.
timeout: Tomorrow's drummer gets the same template and nobody checking it.

hints.text: Would this still get done if you weren't here?

items.note: Draft decision (DR-S10E03). Option B needs Team at LIMITED or better.

options.label: Nobody — it was a one-off
options.result: The session drummer's snare sounds thin by eleven.
options.consequence: It wasn't a one-off; it was a template.

options.label: Put the kit sheet in the studio runbook — distances, polarity per channel, a mono check in the template — and teach Pim to run the phase check himself while you stay at the back
options.result: Tomorrow Pim runs it, tape measure and all. Maya says nothing until he asks.
options.consequence: Written down, and owned by someone who'll be here when you're not.

options.label: You run the phase check yourself every drum day
options.result: It works — while you're here. In four weeks you won't be.
options.consequence: Good outcomes that depend on you being in the room.

options.label: Buy a phase-alignment plug-in and leave it on every drum channel
options.result: It aligns what it's told to — sometimes the wrong drum.

items.text: FIELD NOTE —  When a sound gets worse as mics are added, check the mics’ relationship before the instrument. Polarity is a flip: opposite-facing mics cancel until one is inverted. Distance is a delay: t = d ÷ c, and the comb’s first notch is at 1 ÷ 2Δt. Measure with a tape, equalise, keep spill down with the 3:1 rule, align last, check in mono — and let the player judge the sound.
REFLECTION (optional)  · When something gets worse as more people work on it, what are they each hearing — and when?
